title: A statistical-mechanical framework for mechanically adaptive cytoskeletal organization
problem: Cells remodel their cytoskeleton in response to mechanical cues, but it is unclear why continuous changes in the mechanical environment (substrate stiffness, cellular tension) produce discrete distinct intracellular architectures rather than a smooth continuum of structural variation. What minimal physical principle selects between qualitatively different cytoskeletal organizations?
setting: A minimal coarse-grained model rather than a molecularly detailed one. Alternative cytoskeletal organizations are treated as statistical ensembles of microscopic configurations; a single scalar control parameter (cellular tension, taken to increase with substrate stiffness) is varied. Model predictions are compared against measured correlation length and anisotropy in senescent human fibroblasts across a stiffness range. Only the abstract was available for extraction.
method: Build a statistical-mechanical model in which the free energy balances configurational entropy of the filament/bundle arrangement against mechanically dependent interaction energies between cytoskeletal elements. Sweep the tension control parameter and locate the parameter values at which the favoured ensemble changes character. The model yields three successive structural transitions identified with stress-fibre formation, stress-fibre alignment, and lateral aggregation of fibres, and predicts how correlation length and orientational anisotropy evolve along the tension axis.
contribution: Shows that three qualitatively distinct, experimentally documented cytoskeletal architectures and their stiffness-ordered appearance can emerge from a single minimal free-energy competition between configurational entropy and mechanically tuned interaction energies, without invoking organization-specific molecular machinery. The predicted transition sequence matches measured correlation-length and anisotropy trends in senescent fibroblasts, and its preservation despite altered cell physiology is argued to indicate a robust physical (rather than cell-state-specific) principle.

mathematical_objects.name: canonical ensemble
mathematical_objects.role: Each candidate cytoskeletal organization is represented as an ensemble of microscopic configurations with Boltzmann-weighted statistical selection; this is the framework's core representational move.

mathematical_objects.name: configurational entropy
mathematical_objects.role: The disordering term in the free energy; its competition with interaction energy is what makes the selection between architectures nontrivial.

mathematical_objects.name: free energy minimization
mathematical_objects.role: The selection principle: the realized architecture minimizes energy minus temperature times entropy, so a smooth change in the mechanical energy can move the minimizer discontinuously between ensembles.
mathematical_objects.evidence: Abstract: "allowing configurational entropy to compete with mechanically dependent interaction energies" — an explicit free-energy trade-off whose minimizer selects the favoured ensemble, though the words "free energy" are not used in the abstract.

mathematical_objects.name: phase transition
mathematical_objects.role: Explains discreteness: as the tension control parameter is swept the favoured ensemble changes character abruptly at three values, giving three distinct architectures rather than a continuum.
mathematical_objects.evidence: Abstract: "predicts three successive structural transitions corresponding to stress fiber formation, alignment, and lateral aggregation" placed "on a common cellular-tension axis" — discrete changes of the equilibrium state as a control parameter is swept, i.e. transitions in the statistical-mechanics sense.

mathematical_objects.name: nematic order parameter
mathematical_objects.role: The observable that distinguishes the aligned ensemble from the unaligned one and that the model predicts as a function of tension; measured in the fibroblast data as anisotropy.
mathematical_objects.evidence: Abstract: the alignment transition and "our measurements of ... anisotropy" — the degree of common filament orientation is an orientational (nematic) order parameter, the natural observable distinguishing the aligned from the unaligned ensemble.

mathematical_objects.name: correlation length
mathematical_objects.role: Observable used to test the model: predicted to grow across the transition sequence and compared directly to fibroblast measurements.

limitations: Only the abstract was available; the form of the interaction energy, the configurational degrees of freedom (lattice vs off-lattice, orientational vs positional), the entropy estimate, and whether the 'transitions' are genuine singularities or smooth crossovers are all unspecified in the extracted text.
The mapping from the model's tension control parameter to substrate stiffness is asserted, not derived; the comparison to experiment rests on this assumed monotone relationship.

Empirical validation is a single cell type (senescent fibroblasts) and two summary statistics (correlation length, anisotropy); the claim of a 'robust physical principle' generalizing across cell states is stronger than one cell line supports.
A minimal model matching a qualitative transition ordering is weak evidence for mechanism — other energy functions could produce the same three-stage sequence.
No quantitative goodness-of-fit, parameter identifiability, or comparison against alternative models is described in the abstract.
open_questions: What are the microscopic degrees of freedom and the explicit interaction energy, and does the model reduce to a known lattice model (Ising/Potts, Lebwohl-Lasher nematic, or a bundling model)?
Are the three transitions true phase transitions in some thermodynamic limit, or finite-size crossovers, and what plays the role of system size for a single cell?
Does the same free-energy competition predict the reverse sequence on stiffness reduction, and the hysteresis or timescales of remodelling?
How does the tension-to-stiffness map arise from cell-substrate mechanics, and can it be measured independently?
cross_domain_note: Equilibrium statistical mechanics (lattice models, order-disorder transitions, orientational ordering) applied to a cell-biological mechanism. The entropy-versus-interaction-energy competition and the order-parameter / correlation-length language connect directly to probability's work on Gibbs measures and phase transitions in interacting particle systems.

title: ProteinZero: Self-Improving Protein Generation via Online Reinforcement Learning
problem: Inverse-folding models (generate an amino-acid sequence that folds to a given backbone) are capped by the small, biased pool of paired sequence-structure data in the PDB and by a mismatch between the supervised training objective (sequence recovery) and real design goals (the sequence must actually be designable, thermodynamically stable, and diverse). How can an inverse-folding model keep improving past its supervised ceiling without new labelled data?
setting: Fixed-backbone protein sequence design. A pretrained inverse-folding model is treated as a policy that emits sequences conditioned on a target backbone. Online reinforcement learning with model-generated data and computationally cheap surrogate rewards; no curated preference dataset. Evaluated on the CATH-4.3 benchmark against ProteinMPNN, ESM-IF and InstructPLM, with held-out oracles (ESMFold, AlphaFold3, FoldX, Rosetta). A full run fits on one 8-GPU node in three days.
method: Cast fixed-backbone design as an online RL fine-tuning problem. The reward combines (i) a designability signal from ESMFold refolding and (ii) a self-derived stability (ddG) score computed from the inverse-folding model's own backbone-conditioned sequence likelihoods normalized by unconditional priors, avoiding physics-based energy calculations. The objective balances the multi-reward term, a KL-divergence penalty to the pretrained reference policy, and an embedding-space diversity regularizer that penalizes representational collapse. The design space of RL algorithms (GRPO, RAFT, DPO, multi-round DPO), reward compositions, and regularizers is swept to find configurations that are stable across many rounds of self-generated data.
contribution: A complete, compute-efficient online RL pipeline for inverse folding that self-improves from its own outputs across many rounds without labelled data, cutting design failure rates 36-48% versus ProteinMPNN / ESM-IF / InstructPLM and exceeding 90% success across diverse folds. Two components are the notable pieces: a ddG surrogate derived from the model's own conditional/unconditional likelihood ratio, and a diversity regularizer acting in protein-embedding space rather than sequence space to prevent mode collapse under online RL.

mathematical_objects.name: policy-gradient reinforcement learning
mathematical_objects.role: The inverse-folding model is the policy; sequences are actions rewarded by surrogate designability/stability signals, and the policy is updated online on its own generations.

mathematical_objects.name: Kullback-Leibler divergence
mathematical_objects.role: Anchors the fine-tuned policy to the pretrained reference so reward optimization does not destroy the learned sequence prior; one of the three terms in the objective.

mathematical_objects.name: Group Relative Policy Optimization
mathematical_objects.role: The concrete policy-optimization algorithms compared; GRPO-style group- relative advantage estimation is used to turn scalar rewards into updates without a learned value function.

mathematical_objects.name: multi-objective scalarization
mathematical_objects.role: Combines designability, stability and diversity into a single scalar reward so a single policy balances competing design criteria.

mathematical_objects.name: pointwise mutual information
aliases: backbone-conditioned likelihood normalized by unconditional prior
mathematical_objects.role: The self-derived ddG / stability estimator: scoring a residue or sequence by log P(sequence | backbone) minus log P(sequence) turns the model's own probabilities into a cheap proxy for folding free-energy difference.
mathematical_objects.evidence: Intro contribution 2: "a self-derived ddG estimator computed from the inverse folding model using backbone-conditioned likelihoods normalized by unconditional priors" — a conditional-over-marginal likelihood ratio, i.e. pointwise mutual information between sequence and structure.

mathematical_objects.name: diversity regularization
mathematical_objects.role: Penalizes low dispersion of generated sequences in protein-embedding space to keep the online-RL policy from collapsing onto a few high-reward modes while preserving functional coherence.

mathematical_objects.name: conditional generative model
mathematical_objects.role: The biological object being optimized: a distribution over amino-acid sequences given a fixed backbone geometry, whose samples must refold to that backbone.

limitations: All evaluation is in silico; success is measured by refolding oracles (ESMFold, AlphaFold3, FoldX, Rosetta), not by experiment, so 'success rates above 90%' means agreement with structure predictors, and reward-hacking of those same predictor families is a live concern despite the held-out-oracle checks.

The ddG surrogate is derived from the very model being trained; using a likelihood ratio from the policy as its own stability reward risks a self-reinforcing bias that the held-out FoldX/Rosetta numbers only partially rule out.

Gains are reported as relative failure-rate reductions on one benchmark (CATH-4.3); absolute designability of the baselines and the distribution of hard cases are needed to judge how much headroom is actually being closed.
The Discussion section was not present in the extracted text (only an empty 'Discussion' heading), so ablation magnitudes, the diversity-regularizer form, and failure analyses are not captured here.
'Continuous self-improvement' is demonstrated over a finite number of rounds within a three-day run; whether improvement saturates, oscillates, or drifts over longer horizons is not established.
open_questions: Does the conditional-minus-marginal likelihood ratio correlate with measured ddG well enough to be a stability reward, or only well enough to rank sequences the model already likes?
How does embedding-space diversity regularization compare to explicit determinantal / repulsive-point-process objectives for controlling mode collapse in sequence generation?
Do the RL-optimized sequences transfer to wet-lab expression and stability, or are the gains specific to the oracle ensemble used during training?
Can the same online-RL loop be applied to structure-generating (not just inverse-folding) models without the KL anchor collapsing exploration?
cross_domain_note: Reinforcement-learning methodology (policy gradients, KL-regularized policy optimization, multi-objective reward design, mode-collapse control) applied to a protein-design problem where the biology — designability, folding free energy, functional sequence diversity — supplies the reward structure. The ddG-as-likelihood-ratio move is a clean instance of a biological quantity recovered as pointwise mutual information. Ambiguous flag [ml-bio-benchmark-load-bearing]: the RL machinery is general, but the reward design is biology-specific.

title: Evolutionary Curriculum Learning Improves Biological Sequence Modeling
problem: Variational autoencoders trained on multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) are used as generative models for tasks like missense-variant pathogenicity prediction and functional RNA design. Standard training samples MSA rows uniformly, treating homologous sequences as exchangeable and ignoring that they span a continuum of evolutionary distances. Can the phylogenetic structure of an MSA be used to order training and improve downstream performance?
setting: MSA-based generative modeling. Two architecturally distinct VAEs (EVE for protein variant-effect prediction, RfamGen for RNA family sequence generation), five random seeds per configuration. Evaluation: ClinVar classification AUROC on three proteins (p53, PTEN, SCN5A) and covariance-model bit scores on three RNA families. Effect sizes are small relative to seed variance; most single comparisons do not reach p < 0.05. Requires an O(N^2) pairwise-distance preprocessing step.
method: Evolutionary Curriculum Learning (ECL): a plug-in change to minibatch sampling only, no architecture change. Pick a random anchor sequence; draw minibatches from its neighborhood of evolutionarily similar sequences; expand that neighborhood over training according to a power-law schedule, so the model sees easy (locally consistent, close) sequences first and hard (divergent) sequences later. Pairwise evolutionary distances are computed once in preprocessing. Ablated against fixed-size neighborhood sampling and uniform random sampling.
contribution: Introduces evolutionary distance as a data-derived, annotation-free difficulty measure for curriculum learning on biological sequences, and shows a consistent-direction improvement across two modalities and two models: ClinVar AUROC 0.981 to 0.989 for p53, and stabilization of PTEN (baseline mean 0.905 with runs as low as 0.54; ECL reaches 1.000 every seed); RNA CM bit scores up on all three families, better in 12 of 15 runs. Ablation shows progressive neighborhood expansion beats both fixed-size and uniform sampling.

mathematical_objects.name: variational autoencoder
mathematical_objects.role: The generative model class being trained on MSAs; ECL changes only the order in which its training examples are presented, not its objective or architecture.

mathematical_objects.name: curriculum learning
mathematical_objects.role: The training paradigm instantiated: training examples are ordered by a difficulty measure and the model is exposed to harder examples over time.

mathematical_objects.name: phylogenetic distance
mathematical_objects.role: The difficulty measure and the ordering key: distance from a sampled anchor defines which sequences are 'easy' (close) versus 'hard' (divergent), and determines minibatch membership.

mathematical_objects.name: exchangeability
mathematical_objects.role: The assumption being rejected: the paper argues MSA rows are not exchangeable because they are related by a latent tree, so uniform i.i.d. minibatch sampling is the wrong inductive bias and phylogenetic reweighting is only a partial fix.

mathematical_objects.name: power-law schedule
mathematical_objects.role: Sets the rate at which the sampled neighborhood around the anchor grows over training; the ablated design choice that outperforms fixed-size neighborhoods.

mathematical_objects.name: covariance model
mathematical_objects.role: The RNA evaluation instrument: generated RNA sequences are scored by their bit score under a covariance model of the target family, a profile SCFG capturing sequence and secondary-structure constraints.

limitations: The authors themselves flag that effect sizes are modest relative to seed variance: with five seeds, most individual comparisons do not reach p < 0.05, and the strongest evidence is directional consistency plus ablations, not any headline number.
Only three proteins and three RNA families are evaluated — too few to support generality claims, as the paper states.

Clinical evaluation sets are small and imbalanced (PTEN retains two benign variants, SCN5A none after intersecting labels with modeled positions), so protein AUROC saturates and is a coarse instrument; the dramatic PTEN numbers rest on a near-degenerate label set.
The RNA aggregate result (12/15 runs, p = 0.035) uses the training run as the unit of inference; family-level tests over three families cannot reach significance.
Curriculum requires an O(N^2) pairwise-distance preprocessing step, limiting scaling to large MSAs.
Only VAE architectures are tested; whether the local-to-global principle helps non-VAE (e.g. autoregressive or MSA-transformer) models is untested.
open_questions: Does ECL's benefit come from the curriculum ordering per se, or from implicitly upweighting near-anchor sequences in a way phylogenetic reweighting could also achieve?
Which evolutionary distance metric (Hamming, model-based substitution distance, tree-path distance) is optimal, and how sensitive is the effect to that choice?
Can the O(N^2) preprocessing be replaced by tree-guided sampling directly from an inferred phylogeny?
Does the same local-to-global schedule help autoregressive protein language models or MSA transformers?
cross_domain_note: Curriculum learning (pacing functions, difficulty ordering) crossed with phylogenetics: the explicit rejection of exchangeability for MSA rows, and the use of evolutionary distance as an ordering key, connect to probability's treatment of exchangeable vs tree-structured dependent samples (de Finetti, coalescent) and to statistics' phylogenetic-reweighting / effective-sample- size corrections. Ambiguous flags [ml-bio-benchmark-load-bearing] and [popgen-phylo-theory]: the phylogenetic structure is load-bearing to the method, though the paper uses it heuristically rather than through explicit coalescent/tree models.

title: Probing and steering biology across Boltz-1's trunk-diffusion boundary
problem: AlphaFold3-class structure predictors have a representational trunk (processes sequence and evolutionary context) feeding a diffusion module (generates atomic coordinates). What biological information is present on each side of that architectural boundary, is that information actually used causally, and do standard interpretability evaluations measure it faithfully?
setting: Per-residue activations from the Pairformer trunk and the diffusion module of Boltz-1. Probing against dense secondary-structure labels (DSSP) and sparse curated annotations (SwissProt: signal peptides, disulfide bonds, amino-acid identity). Analysis tools: supervised linear probes, sparse autoencoders, and causal interventions on the final trunk single representation that conditions diffusion. Interventions are compared to matched-norm random directions. Trained SAEs, activations and code are released.
method: Train linear probes on activations from each module to test linear decodability of geometric and sequence-chemical features. Train sparse autoencoders on the same activations to extract candidate monosemantic features. Then intervene: add a probe-derived direction (helix, coil, strand) to the trunk's single representation with varying magnitude and measure the dose-dependent change in predicted structure against matched-norm random controls. Separately, re-score probes against sparse vs dense label sets to quantify how missing annotations inflate the apparent false-positive rate.
contribution: Shows the trunk keeps both geometry and sequence chemistry linearly decodable, while the diffusion module preserves geometry but strongly attenuates chemistry — evidence the two modules expose different information. Demonstrates that linear decodability does not imply causal influence: a strand direction with F1 = 0.82 produces no measurable change in strand content under intervention, whereas helix and coil directions steer structure dose-dependently. Shows scoring interpretability units against sparse annotations turns correct-but-unlabelled predictions into false positives, so such scores are lower bounds. Finds supervised probes beat single SAE features wherever a label exists.

mathematical_objects.name: linear probe
mathematical_objects.role: Primary measurement instrument: a linear map from per-residue activations to a biological label, whose accuracy is taken as a measure of how linearly accessible that concept is in a given module's representation.

mathematical_objects.name: sparse dictionary learning
mathematical_objects.role: Unsupervised decomposition of activations into an overcomplete set of sparsely-active features, used to search for monosemantic directions without labels; found less reliable than supervised probes for known concepts.

mathematical_objects.name: causal intervention
mathematical_objects.role: Tests whether a decodable direction is used: the direction is added to the trunk single representation and the resulting change in predicted structure is measured, isolating causal from merely correlational signal.

mathematical_objects.name: linear representation hypothesis
mathematical_objects.role: The organizing assumption: biological concepts correspond to directions in activation space that can be both read out by projection and written by addition; the paper's central finding is that readability and writability of a direction come apart.
mathematical_objects.evidence: Abstract/intro: "test whether decodable directions can steer the model", "Helix and coil directions change predicted structure dose-dependently against matched-norm random controls", "supervised probes ... provide more reliable steering directions" — concepts treated throughout as linear directions.

mathematical_objects.name: dose-response curve
mathematical_objects.role: The causal-effect readout: predicted secondary-structure content is plotted against intervention magnitude, and a monotone increase relative to matched-norm random controls is the evidence of causal influence.

mathematical_objects.name: evaluation under incomplete labels
mathematical_objects.role: Explains a systematic bias in interpretability metrics: when only some true positives are annotated, a correct prediction on an unannotated residue is scored as a false positive, so measured precision/F1 are lower bounds rather than estimates.
mathematical_objects.evidence: Abstract: "probes also score markedly lower against sparse SwissProt annotations than against dense DSSP labels, because unannotated residues that the model gets right are charged as false positives; such scores are therefore lower bounds."

mathematical_objects.name: diffusion model
mathematical_objects.role: One of the two representational regimes analyzed: the coordinate- generating module whose per-residue activations retain geometry but lose sequence chemistry.

limitations: Interventions modify only the final trunk single representation s; the pair representation z is never touched, so the null result for the strand direction is confounded with 'strand information may live in z' — the paper acknowledges this but cannot resolve it.

Findings are for one model (Boltz-1); the trunk/diffusion contrast is plausibly architecture-specific and the paper's generalization claims to AlphaFold3-class models rest on concurrent work, not its own experiments.

Steering success is measured by change in the model's own predicted structure, not by physical plausibility or experimental structure, so 'inducible' means 'the predictor's output moves', not 'a real helix forms'.
Probe F1 and SAE feature scores against sparse labels are explicitly only lower bounds; the true decodability of sparsely-annotated features (signal peptides, disulfides) is not pinned down.
SAE-vs-probe comparison is restricted to concepts that already have labels, by construction; it says nothing about the setting where SAEs are supposed to help (unlabelled features).
open_questions: Does intervening directly on the pair representation z induce beta-strand content, confirming that strand information is pairwise rather than single-residue?
Why does sequence chemistry fade across diffusion layers — is it genuinely consumed to compute geometry, or re-encoded in a form linear probes miss?
Can the missing-label correction be formalized (e.g. as positive-unlabeled learning) to give unbiased decodability estimates rather than lower bounds?
Do helix and coil really sit at opposite ends of one linear axis, and is that a property of Boltz-1 or of secondary-structure geometry generally?
cross_domain_note: Mechanistic-interpretability methodology (linear probes, sparse dictionary learning, causal interventions, the linear representation hypothesis) applied where the biology is load-bearing: the concepts probed and steered are secondary structure, signal peptides, disulfide bonds. The missing-label bias is a positive-unlabeled / censored-data problem that statistics has studied properly. The decodability-without-causality result is a clean cross-domain cautionary case.

title: Task- and dataset-specific information in protein language models
problem: Protein language models (PLMs) are used as feature extractors: an amino-acid sequence is mapped to embeddings that feed downstream predictors. By convention the last-layer embedding is used, on the assumption that depth monotonically improves representations. Is that assumption right for self-supervised PLMs, and if not, what determines which layer carries the information a given downstream task needs?
setting: 13 PLMs from five model families across four architectures; 15 downstream tasks drawn from 11 datasets, spanning per-residue tasks (secondary structure, contacts) and whole-protein tasks (localization, solubility, stability, fluorescence, homology). Datasets split into deep-mutational-scan (DMS) type (many variants of one or few proteins) and diverse-natural-protein type. Includes artificial proteins (Rosetta-designed, ProGen-generated lysozymes). Analysis is layer-wise probing plus latent-space geometry.
method: For every PLM and every layer, train a probe model on that layer's embeddings for each downstream task and compare probe performance across layers. In parallel, compute geometric descriptors of each layer's latent space (intrinsic dimension, neighborhood overlap between consecutive layers) to characterize how representations evolve with depth. Relate the layer-vs- performance profile to (i) similarity between the masked-language-modeling pretraining objective and the downstream objective and (ii) dataset type. Repeat on artificial-protein tasks.
contribution: Systematic evidence that the last layer of a PLM is rarely the best layer for a downstream task. Identifies two determinants of where the useful information sits: objective mismatch (residue-level tasks, close to the MLM objective, improve monotonically with depth; whole-protein tasks do not) and dataset type (DMS datasets are best served by shallow layers, diverse-protein datasets by deep layers). Shows PLM performance drops sharply on artificial proteins even when they are verified functional, arguing PLMs accumulate an abstraction of naturally evolved sequence space, not of protein function per se.

mathematical_objects.name: linear classifier probe
mathematical_objects.role: Primary instrument: per-layer probe accuracy on a downstream task is the operational measure of how much task-relevant information that layer's embedding exposes.

mathematical_objects.name: intrinsic dimension
mathematical_objects.role: Geometric descriptor of each layer's latent space, used to characterize how the representation expands and contracts with depth independently of any label.

mathematical_objects.name: neighborhood overlap
mathematical_objects.role: Measures how much the local neighbor structure of a sequence is preserved between consecutive layers, tracking where representational change concentrates; used to show shallow and deep layers can resemble each other under MLM training.

mathematical_objects.name: masked language modeling
mathematical_objects.role: The pretraining objective whose (mis)alignment with a downstream objective is the paper's explanatory variable for the shape of the layer-vs- performance curve.

mathematical_objects.name: objective mismatch
mathematical_objects.role: The main explanatory construct: the larger the gap between the local token-level MLM objective and a global protein-level downstream objective, the earlier in the network the peak-performing layer sits and the more information is 'diluted' in deeper layers.
mathematical_objects.evidence: Conclusion: "The first factor is the difference between the pre-training and the downstream objectives. For residue-level tasks, the difference is lower than for protein-level ones, so PLMs tend to improve monotonically on such tasks."

mathematical_objects.name: k-nearest-neighbor density estimate
mathematical_objects.role: Cited and extended construct for judging embedding quality: an embedding's reliability is scored by the fraction of randomized non-biological sequences among its latent-space nearest neighbors — a k-NN-based out-of-distribution / density statistic — which the paper tracks across layers.
mathematical_objects.evidence: Intro: "They quantify the uncertainty of a protein embedding by the fraction of randomized non-biological sequences among its latent-space neighbors ... how does the distinction between natural and artificially designed proteins change across a network's layers?"

limitations: Findings are correlational: 'objective mismatch' and 'dataset type' are post-hoc groupings that co-vary (DMS datasets are both narrow and stability/fitness-oriented), and the paper does not disentangle them experimentally.
Probe performance conflates information content with linear accessibility; a deep layer could hold the information non-linearly and score worse.

The artificial-protein conclusion rests on two generation engines (Rosetta, ProGen lysozymes) and a small set of designed sequences; 'PLMs abstract evolved sequence space, not function' is a broad claim from a narrow sample.
Practical guidance ('use intermediate layers') depends on having a labelled validation set to pick the layer, which is the same data bottleneck that motivates using PLMs in the first place.
No single best layer generalizes; the result is a heterogeneity finding, so the actionable output is a procedure, not a recommendation.
open_questions: Can objective mismatch be quantified a priori (before probing) to predict the best layer for a new task?
Do autoregressive PLMs show the same shallow-layer advantage on DMS data, or is it specific to the MLM input-reconstruction geometry?
Is the artificial-protein performance drop a representational limit or a training-distribution artifact that more diverse pretraining would remove?
Does combining layers (learned weighting) recover the per-task optimum without a labelled layer-selection step?
cross_domain_note: Representation-analysis methodology (probing classifiers, intrinsic dimension, neighborhood overlap, k-NN OOD scoring) applied to protein language models, with the biology load-bearing: the residue-vs-protein task split and the natural-vs-designed protein contrast are what structure the findings. The 'fraction of random neighbors' score is a k-NN density / two-sample statistic under a biological name.

title: Leveraging generative hallucination and biophysics-informed modeling for unified biomolecular sequence-structure co-design
problem: De novo design of biomolecular interactions (protein-protein, protein-ligand, and especially protein-nucleic-acid and nucleic-acid-nucleic-acid complexes) is hard: sequence and structure are tightly coupled, physics-based energy functions are brittle under local optimization, and learned methods generalize poorly across modalities with scarce complex data. Can pretrained folding and inverse-folding models be coordinated at inference time — with no fine-tuning and no backprop through them — to co-design sequence and structure across modalities?
setting: Inference-only, all-atom sequence-structure co-design. Pretrained folding (AlphaFold3-style all-atom diffusion) and modality-specific inverse-folding models are treated as frozen black-box operators; only their outputs (sequences, structures, confidence/feasibility scalars) are used. A fixed inference budget (number of expensive folding calls) is allocated by search. Evaluated on protein-RNA, protein-DNA, protein-protein and protein-ligand design under matched compute budgets, with held-out AlphaFold3 and Chai-1 evaluation and a multi-expert variant using Boltz-2 + AlphaFold2 jointly. Evaluation is entirely computational; no wet-lab validation.
method: MCTH (Monte Carlo Tree Hallucination): frame co-design as finite-budget planning over hallucinated sequence-structure states. Nodes are candidate sequence-structure states; frozen folding and inverse-folding models propose transitions (hallucinate a structure from an underspecified sequence, redesign the sequence from that structure). Monte Carlo Tree Search runs selection / expansion / simulation / backup to allocate the folding budget across competing design trajectories, with the value signal combining model confidence, predictive uncertainty, cross-expert consensus/disagreement (when multiple predictors are available), and optional biophysical feasibility terms (steric, thermodynamic, energy-like). No component model is fine-tuned or differentiated through.
contribution: A single inference-time planning layer, shared across protein-RNA, protein-DNA, protein-protein and protein-ligand design, that turns hallucination-based cycling into adaptive tree search over a fixed folding budget. Under matched budgets it beats fixed-schedule cycling and independent best-of-N sampling, and improvements transfer to held-out predictors (AlphaFold3, Chai-1) not used during search. Integrates biophysical feasibility signals into the same decision loop rather than as post-hoc filtering, and supports multiple folding experts through consensus/disagreement signals.

mathematical_objects.name: Monte Carlo tree search
mathematical_objects.role: The planner: it allocates a fixed budget of expensive folding evaluations across competing sequence-structure design trajectories, expanding promising branches and backing up value estimates.

mathematical_objects.name: upper confidence bound for trees
mathematical_objects.role: The node-selection rule inside MCTS: balances exploiting high-value design trajectories against exploring under-visited ones, using an uncertainty/visit-count bonus.
mathematical_objects.evidence: Intro: MCTS "adaptively allocate expensive folding evaluations across competing sequence--structure trajectories" and the framework is described as managing "exploration--exploitation balance" during selection, expansion and backup — the standard UCT selection mechanism, though UCT/UCB is not named.

mathematical_objects.name: finite-horizon planning
mathematical_objects.role: The framing: design is cast as uncertainty-aware planning over states (hallucinated sequence-structure pairs) with a fixed action/evaluation budget, replacing fixed-schedule cycling.

mathematical_objects.name: query-by-committee
mathematical_objects.role: When several folding predictors are available, their agreement is used as a value signal and their disagreement as an uncertainty signal guiding where to spend budget — the query-by-committee principle applied to design state evaluation.
mathematical_objects.evidence: Abstract: "incorporating model confidence and uncertainty, as well as cross-expert consensus/disagreement when multiple predictors are available"; intro: "Multiple folding experts can be combined through consensus, disagreement, and uncertainty signals."

mathematical_objects.name: generative hallucination
mathematical_objects.role: The proposal mechanism: feeding underspecified inputs (all-X sequences, partial complexes) to a diffusion folding model yields plausible conformations from its learned prior, which become candidate states in the tree.

mathematical_objects.name: denoising diffusion model
mathematical_objects.role: The frozen folding operator whose hallucinated samples and confidence scores drive the search; its all-atom scope is what makes the method work across nucleic-acid and ligand modalities.

mathematical_objects.name: derivative-free optimization
mathematical_objects.role: The design constraint and paradigm: component models are optimized around, not through — only their scalar outputs are used, no gradients, no fine-tuning — so search must do all the work of navigating the sequence-structure landscape.

limitations: Evaluation is entirely in silico; the paper states wet-lab validation is future work, so 'improves over simpler sampling' means improves on predicted-structure metrics, and reward-hacking of the folding oracles is not ruled out despite held-out AlphaFold3/Chai-1 checks.

Matched-budget comparisons are against fixed cycling and best-of-N; there is no comparison to gradient-based hallucination (BindCraft, BoltzDesign) at matched wall-clock, only the argument that those are expensive and initialization-sensitive.

The biophysical feasibility terms are 'optional' and 'energy-like'; the extract does not quantify how much of the gain comes from search versus from adding physics, nor which modalities benefit from which.

Nucleic-acid design is the stated motivation but complex training data for the frozen models is itself scarce and heterogeneous, so the frozen operators may be weak exactly where the method is most needed.
MCTS cost and the branching/rollout design are not visible in the extracted sections; 'fixed inference budget' is compared across methods but the absolute number of folding calls is not given here.
open_questions: How much of the improvement is the tree search itself versus the biophysical feasibility signals — do the two help the same modalities?
Does adaptive search still win against gradient-based hallucination at matched wall-clock, or only against schedule-based cycling?
Can the consensus/disagreement signal be calibrated so that expert agreement actually predicts experimental success rather than shared predictor bias?
What state representation and rollout policy make MCTS tractable for long chains and large assemblies where the tree branching explodes?
cross_domain_note: Planning and search methodology (MCTS, UCT-style exploration-exploitation, query-by-committee ensemble uncertainty, derivative-free optimization) applied to biomolecular co-design where the biology is load-bearing: all-atom folding priors, modality-specific inverse folding, and biophysical feasibility (base stacking, ion coordination, steric clash) supply the state space and value function. The consensus/disagreement value signal is query-by-committee under a biological name.
